Ancient Rome. This civilization and empire spanned roughly twelve hundred years from around seven hundred fifty-three BCE to four hundred seventy-six CE, beginning as a small settlement on the Tiber River and evolving into the ancient world's most powerful military and political force. Rome's republican institutions, legal systems, engineering achievements, and territorial expansion across the Mediterranean and beyond profoundly shaped Western civilization, while its adoption of Christianity transformed the religion into a global force.

Rome traditionally dates its founding to seven hundred fifty-three BCE. Early Rome was a monarchy before an aristocratic revolution in five hundred nine BCE established the Republic, featuring consuls, a Senate, and eventually democratic assemblies balancing power. The Republic expanded through conquest as the Punic Wars from two hundred sixty-four to one hundred forty-six BCE destroyed Carthage, the Mediterranean's rival power. Rome conquered Greece in one hundred forty-six BCE and Egypt in thirty BCE, and vast territories across Europe, Asia, and North Africa. The toga became the quintessential symbol of Roman civic identity and status as the quality and style of one's toga indicated social rank, and the right to wear it distinguished citizens from non-citizens.

Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul from fifty-eight to fifty BCE and subsequent civil war ended the Republic. His adopted heir Augustus, living from sixty-three BCE to fourteen CE, established the Empire, creating a system of autocracy veiled under republican forms. Roman engineering transformed the ancient world as aqueducts transported water to cities, roads facilitated trade and military movement, concrete enabled monumental architecture like the Colosseum and Pantheon, and sophisticated plumbing served urban centers. The legal system, codified into principles and procedures, became the foundation of Western legal traditions as concepts like contracts, property, and citizenship rights originated in Roman jurisprudence.

Rome eventually Christianized, with Christianity becoming official in three hundred eighty CE. The Christian Church became institutionally intertwined with Roman authority, and as the Empire fragmented in four hundred seventy-six CE, the Church preserved Roman institutional and intellectual traditions.
